newsitem.title: Cyprus: Cyprus stocks recover despite tensions.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus stocks recover despite tensions.

text.p: The Cyprus Stock Market (CSE), buoyed by renewed optimism, has risen six percent in the past month, recovering losses suffered shortly after the offical launch of the bourse in March this year.
The 41-share CSE all-share index closed at 88.00 points on Friday at the end of the week's trading, scoring a marginal increase of 0.13 points, or 0.14 percent over last Friday's close of 87.87.
"Prices are continuing their ascent," said Theodoulos Charalambides, Laiki Investments general manager. "I think the trend will continue even if there may be some ups and downs in the meantime."

CSE sector indices have risen steadily in the past month, unaffected by heightened tensions on the divided island after the killings of two Greek Cypriots by Turks during protests last month, and American strikes against Iraq this week.
"This proves the confidence people have in the performance of the economy and in the prospects for the rest of the year, and perhaps even 1997," Charalambides told Reuters.
Two months ago the index was moving at around 82 points in thin trade, with the market jittery soon after its official launch on March 29 after years of unofficial over-the-counter trading.

The Bank of Cyprus closed at 3.58, up 1.5 cents from last week's close of 3.565. The Cyprus Popular Bank gained seven cents to close at 3.355 and the Hellenic Bank closed at 3.035, up 10.5 cents from last week's close of 2.93.

In the insurance sector Universal Life made considerable gains to close at 4.24, up 26.5 cents from last week's close of 3.975. Paneuropean Insurance closed at 1.515, shedding five cents from 1.565 last week.
Shares of F.W. Woolworth (Cyprus) and Zako Ltd retreated. Woolworth lost three cents to close at 1.045 and Zako 5.5 cents to close at 1.06.
Earlier this week Woolworth made a successful bid to take over the remaining 45 percent of Zako, a cosmetics and accessories outlet, in a one-for-one share swap.
Mary Demetriou, a broker at the Cyprus Investment and Securities Corporation (CISCO) a member of the Bank of Cyprus Group said prices were firming, without indications of any drastic changes.

Demetriou said she expected a brief static period since listed companies would be collecting payments on partly-paid shares and new share issues, expected to reach 16 million pounds ($34.7 million) this year.
"I think it will be a good year. It won't be spectacular, it definitely won't be like 1995 which was the golden year of the market but there is going to be a move up," she told Reuters.

Laiki Investment's report said the market capitalisation of all listed companies was 1.12 billion pounds at 30 August 1996 compared to 1.06 billion pounds at the end of June 1996, a rise of 5.2 percent.
Banks, the most actively traded stock on the exchange by far, dominated the market with their capitalisation reaching 59 percent of the total in comparison to 58 percent at the end of June 1996.
Industrial companies came second with 13 percent of total market capitalisation.
Laiki Investments said the total volume of transactions for the first eight months of 1996 was 178.9 million pounds in comparison to 137 million pounds for the whole of 1995.
Half the total volume for this year - 89.5 million pounds - was traded during the first two months of 1996.

In the first eight months of the year Bank of Cyprus and the Cyprus Popular Bank dominated transactions by accounting for more than 55 percent of total volume traded. More than 70 percent of overall trading is concentrated on 10 companies.
